newsitem.title: USA: U.S. set to conclude case against Garcia Abrego.
newsitem.headline: U.S. set to conclude case against Garcia Abrego.

text.p: A trial that revealed the inner workings of Mexico's once-mightiest drug cartel moves into its final week on Monday as the U.S. government concludes its case against accused drug kingpin Juan Garcia Abrego.

Final prosecution witnesses were expected to testify on Monday, followed by what defence attorneys say will be no more than a day of testimony on behalf of Garcia Abrego. After closing arguments, the case will go to the jury.
Garcia Abrego, who could face life in prison if convicted of 22 drug-related counts, was not expected to take the stand, although his lawyers would not confirm that.
For prosecutors, the closing days of the three-week trial will bring to an end years of pursuit and painstaking police work to bring Garcia Abrego to justice.

The stakes are high for the U.S. government, which pressured Mexico to help capture Garcia Abrego and made him a symbol of the fight against international drug-trafficking by placing him on the FBI's 10 Most Wanted list.
His Gulf drug cartel, the government said, shipped up to a third of the cocaine consumed in the United States.
The task of catching Garcia Abrego was made difficult by millions of dollars in bribes he allegedly paid to officials in the United States and Mexico to protect the illicit empire.

Throughout the 1980s and early 1990s, the Gulf cartel operated with relative impunity from its base in northern Mexico, bringing in thousands of tons of cocaine from the Cali cartel in Colombia and shipping it to the United States. Estimates of the fortune amassed by Garcia Abrego, a former cookie factory worker from Texas, range up to $15 billion.

Former cartel insiders who turned against the man they called "El Patron" testified that he lavished money and gifts on friendly police and prosecutors all the way from the dusty border town of Matamoros to the halls of power in Mexico City.
His influence once reached at least as high as a deputy Attorney General in charge of Mexico's anti-drug efforts, who was paid $1.5 million a month in bribes, they said.

Witnesses told of how, on the U.S. side, agents at highway checkpoints in Texas were paid off so that drug shipments would be waved through untouched. They also said that members of the U.S. Immigration and Naturalisation Service and the U.S. National Guard were bribed to help ferry drugs from the border on government buses and military trucks.
Garcia Abrego is not charged with murder, but cartel members testified that he ordered the killing of several key aides who got out of line.
According to testimony, it was Garcia Abrego's legacy of violence that led to his Jan. 14 capture in Monterrey, Mexico and subsequent deportation to Houston for trial.

Carlos Resendez, a police commander in the cartel, said he led Mexican drug agents to Garcia Abrego's hideout because, after falling out with the man he had known for 30 years and "loved like a brother," he feared for his life.

The sometimes riveting testimony did not disguise a major problem with the government's case. An FBI agent admitted that, despite more than three years of continuous wiretapping, investigators have no known tapes of Garcia Abrego or even a recording in which his name is mentioned.
Defence attorneys have hammered home that point, using it as the core of their defence that the government has the wrong man, that Garcia Abrego was not the head of the Gulf cartel.
